definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: The self in which, by knowledge, all beings are seen, and then in the Lord (4.35); the yoked yogin sees the self abiding in all beings and all beings in the self (6.29), his self having become the self of all beings (5.7); the controlled mind rests in the self alone (6.18) and, seeing the self by the self, is content in the self (6.20). The same word is used reflexively: one raises oneself by oneself, and the self is one's own friend or enemy (6.5–6).

names.name: divyaṃ janma karma ca (divine birth and action)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: Though unborn, of imperishable self and lord of beings, Kṛṣṇa comes into being (saṃbhavāmi) through his own māyā, presiding over his own prakṛti (4.6); whenever dharma declines and adharma rises he sends himself forth (4.7), age after age, to protect the good, destroy evil-doers and establish dharma (4.8); he has had many births, all of which he knows (4.5); whoever knows his birth and action as divine is not reborn but comes to him (4.9). The word avatāra itself does not occur.

name: The kinds of sacrifice (yajña) in Bhagavad Gītā 4.24–33

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: Sacrifice is extended beyond the fire-rite to a series of offerings, each described in ritual language: all are born of action, destroy impurity, and knowing them frees (4.30, 4.32); of them the sacrifice of knowledge is better than the sacrifice of material things, because all action culminates in knowledge (4.33); those who eat the remainder of sacrifice go to the eternal Brahman (4.31).

members: every factor of the rite seen as Brahman (brahmārpaṇa, 4.24)
sacrifice offered by sacrifice into the fire of Brahman (4.25b)
the senses offered into the fires of restraint (4.26a)
sense-objects offered into the fires of the senses (4.26b)
actions of senses and breath offered into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint kindled by knowledge (4.27)
sacrifice of recitation and of knowledge (svādhyāya-, jñāna-yajña, 4.28)
prāṇa offered into apāna and apāna into prāṇa by those intent on prāṇāyāma (4.29)
breaths offered into breaths by those regulated in food (4.30)
notes: The count of kinds depends on how 4.28's compounds are divided; the list follows the verses in order.

name: The succession of the Gītā's yoga (Kṛṣṇa – Vivasvat – Manu – Ikṣvāku)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: The imperishable yoga was declared by Kṛṣṇa to Vivasvat, by Vivasvat to Manu, by Manu to Ikṣvāku (4.1); received in succession (paramparā) it was known by the royal sages, then lost over a long time (4.2); Kṛṣṇa re-declares the same ancient yoga to Arjuna because he is his devotee and friend — it is the highest secret (4.3).

Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: The noun bhakti does not occur, but Arjuna is taught as the Lord's devotee (bhakta) and friend (4.3); the Lord responds to people in the way they resort to him (4.11); many absorbed in him and taking refuge in him reached his state (4.10); the meditator sits with thought on him and intent on him (6.14); the yogin established in oneness worships him as abiding in all beings (6.31); and of all yogins the one who worships him with faith, inner self gone to him, is the most yoked (6.47).

Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: The goal named in 5.24–26: the yogin whose happiness, delight and light are within, having become Brahman, attains brahma-nirvāṇa (5.24); seers with impurities destroyed, dualities cut, self-restrained and devoted to the welfare of all beings attain it (5.25); for self-knowing ascetics free of desire and anger it is near on every side (5.26). Related expressions in ch. 6: peace culminating in nirvāṇa that abides in the Lord (6.15), becoming Brahman and the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman (6.27–28).

Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: Brahman is every factor of the sacrifice and is what is to be reached (4.24); it is the fire into which sacrifice is offered (4.25); the eternal Brahman is reached by those who eat the remainder of sacrifice (4.31); the yoked sage soon reaches it (5.6); actions are placed in it (5.10); it is flawless and the same, so that those whose mind rests in sameness are established in it (5.19–20); the yogin becomes Brahman (brahma-bhūta) and attains brahma-nirvāṇa and contact with Brahman (5.24, 6.27–28).

Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: Being the same in success and failure (4.22); neither hating nor craving (5.3); seeing a learned brahmin, cow, elephant, dog and dog-eater with an equal eye (5.18); the mind established in sameness, as Brahman is the same (5.19); neither rejoicing at the pleasant nor agitated by the unpleasant (5.20); composure amid cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour (6.7); clod, stone and gold alike (6.8); equal regard toward friend, foe, neutral, good and wicked (6.9); seeing the same everywhere (6.29), by comparison with oneself (6.32). Arjuna calls the yoga taught 'yoga as sāmya' (6.33).

name: The fate of the one fallen from yoga

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: Arjuna asks what becomes of one with faith who does not strive enough and whose mind falls from yoga before perfection — does he perish like a torn cloud, fallen from both (6.37–39)? Kṛṣṇa: there is no destruction for him here or hereafter, for no doer of good goes to a bad end (6.40); he dwells for endless years in the worlds of the meritorious and is reborn in a pure and prosperous house (6.41), or — rarer — in a family of wise yogins (6.42); there he regains the understanding of his former body and strives again (6.43), carried on by his former practice even against his will; even the mere enquirer into yoga passes beyond śabda-brahman (6.44); striving, cleansed, perfected through many births, he reaches the highest course (6.45).

Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: Knowledge is to be learnt from 'the knowers who see the truth' (jñāninas tattvadarśinaḥ), approached with prostration, thorough questioning and service; they will instruct it (4.34). The teaching itself is presented as passed down in succession from Kṛṣṇa (4.1–3). The word guru does not occur in these verses.

Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: Kṛṣṇa is unborn, of imperishable self and lord of beings, coming into being by his own māyā (4.6); he responds to people as they resort to him (4.11); he made the fourfold class-order yet is the imperishable non-doer (4.13); actions do not stain him and he has no longing for their fruit (4.14); he is the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, great lord of all worlds and friend of all beings (5.29); he is seen everywhere and everything in him (6.30). Whether the 'lord' (prabhu, vibhu) of 5.14–15, who creates no agency and takes on no one's merit or sin, is the supreme Lord or the embodied self is disputed by commentators.

Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: The course of action is deep (4.17); action binds when done from desire with attachment to fruit (5.12), but not when done without attachment, for the sake of sacrifice, with actions placed in Brahman (4.20–23, 5.10); knowledge burns all actions to ashes (4.19, 4.37); all sacrifices are born of action (4.32) and all action culminates in knowledge (4.33); the Lord is not stained by actions and whoever knows this is not bound (4.14).

Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: Even sages are bewildered about what action and inaction are (4.16); one must understand action (karma), vikarma and inaction (akarma), for the course of action is deep (4.17); the wise one sees inaction in action and action in inaction (4.18). The text does not define vikarma.

relations.note: the analysis of action announced in 4.16–18

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: Chs. 4–6 name the goal in several ways: not being born again and coming to the Lord (4.9); release from the inauspicious (4.16); going to the eternal Brahman (4.31, 5.6); supreme peace (4.39, 5.12, 5.29); non-return (apunarāvṛtti, 5.17); brahma-nirvāṇa (5.24–26); being forever free (sadā mukta) while intent on mokṣa (5.28); peace culminating in nirvāṇa (6.15); the highest course (parā gati, 6.45).

name: The body as the city of nine gates (navadvāra pura)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: Having renounced all actions by the mind, the self-controlled embodied one dwells at ease in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action (5.13).

notes: The same image occurs in Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.18 (navadvāre pure dehī).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna have both passed through many births, which Kṛṣṇa knows and Arjuna does not (4.5); whoever knows the Lord's divine birth and action does not go to rebirth on leaving the body (4.9); the one fallen from yoga dwells in the worlds of the meritorious and is reborn, carrying the understanding and practice of his former body (6.41–44), perfected through many births (6.45).

Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: Asked whether renunciation of actions or yoga is better (5.1), Kṛṣṇa says both bring the highest good but the yoga of action is superior (5.2); the constant renouncer is one who neither hates nor craves (5.3); Sāṃkhya and Yoga are one in result (5.4–5); renunciation is hard to attain without yoga (5.6); renouncing all actions by the mind the embodied one dwells at ease (5.13); the renouncer and yogin is one who does required action without depending on its fruit, not one without sacred fires or rites (6.1); what is called renunciation is yoga, for no one becomes a yogin without renouncing intention (6.2).

name: The self as its own friend and enemy

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: One should raise oneself by oneself and not let oneself sink, for the self alone is one's friend and the self alone one's enemy (6.5); the self is a friend to one who has conquered himself by himself, but for one without self-mastery the self acts in enmity like an enemy (6.6).

Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: Chs. 4–6 name the guṇas only in passing: the fourfold class-order was made according to the division of guṇas and actions (4.13); the yogin to whom supreme happiness comes has rajas stilled (6.27).

name: The varṇas by guṇa and action

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā chs. 4–6: The fourfold class-order (cāturvarṇya) was created by the Lord according to the division of guṇa and karma; though its maker, he is the imperishable non-doer (4.13). The verse does not say whether class is fixed by birth.
